summary: Considers how the recipient of network mail can be certain a message is really from the person named in its signature. It presents a general approach to signature authentication and proposes a specific implementation.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 644 proposes using a reserved network socket to identify mail sent by an authorized process. A message marked this way is authenticated with respect to its sending host, not guaranteed trustworthy in every other sense.

questions: how did rfc 644 propose authenticating network mail
subtitle: A proposal for marking network mail authenticated by its source host.

tldr.problem: A receiving host needs a way to distinguish messages sent by an authorized mail process from messages sent by a process pretending to be one.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal reserves agreed source sockets for authorized mail-sending processes; the receiving process marks mail from those sockets as authenticated with respect to the sending host.
tldr.outcome: The sender's host remains responsible for protecting the reserved sockets, and users must judge trust based on that host's authentication and access controls.

today: RFC 644 proposes a socket-based way to mark network mail as authenticated with respect to its sending host.

sections.title: The Network Mail Signature Problem
sections.content: The RFC asks how a recipient can know that a network-mail signature, such as the name in the FROM field, is authentic. It considers a model in which a sending process on one host transfers mail to a receiving process on another host, which places the message in a mailbox. The note assumes that any local-mail signature-authentication problem is handled separately.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can name a sender, but the receiver needs a way to know whether the sending process was allowed to use that name. This proposal focuses on identifying authorized sending processes across hosts.

sections.title: Authenticate the Sending Process by Socket
sections.content:
The proposed approach lets the receiving process mark a message as authenticated with respect to the sending host. The hosts agree in advance which socket or sockets are reserved for authenticated mail. A receiving process treats mail as authenticated only when it comes from one of those sockets.

The sender host must ensure that only authorized mail-sending processes can access the reserved socket. A user should understand that an authenticated mark means the sending host identified the sender; the user's confidence depends on that host's authentication and access-control procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving host checks which socket sent the mail. The mark means the sending host says an authorized mail program used that socket, so trust still depends on the sending host's controls.

sections.title: Why the Proposal Avoids Passwords
sections.content:
The RFC rejects passwords as operationally impractical: a sending program would need access to the password, changing a compromised password would require coordination at both hosts, and pairwise secure mail among N hosts would require N*N passwords.

For a planned TENEX experiment, the RFC lists an ICP “from” socket of 232, FTP user command sockets 234 and 235, and a default data-transfer socket of 237. The plan was to mark incoming messages authenticated only when the connection came from remote socket 232.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors prefer reserved sockets to passwords because programs would need access to passwords and hosts would have to coordinate password changes. The TENEX socket numbers describe a planned experiment in the RFC.
